questions.stem: A FortiGate has a static default route in its routing table, but a conditional-advertisement rule using condition-type exist never matches that default. What is the first thing to verify?

choices.text: The route has been installed in the FIB after policy routing.
choices.feedback: The FIB is not the evaluation table for conditional-advertisement predicates.

choices.text: The peer has accepted the default route in its Adj-RIB-In.
choices.feedback: Peer acceptance is downstream of the local condition evaluation.

choices.text: The default route is present in the BGP RIB as learned or originated.
choices.feedback: Conditional route maps are evaluated against the BGP RIB, not every kernel route.

choices.text: The neighbor has a negotiated four-octet AS capability.
choices.feedback: That capability does not make a static-only prefix visible to the BGP condition map.

questions.stem: A conditional advertisement has two condition route maps. One matches and one does not. The condition type is exist. What should happen?

choices.text: The advertisement is suppressed because the configured conditions are conjunctive.
choices.feedback: All configured condition maps must satisfy the selected condition type; one false condition blocks the gate.

choices.text: The advertisement is sent because one condition matched.
choices.feedback: The condition list is not an OR list; one match is insufficient.

choices.text: The advertisement is sent only if both peers are established.
choices.feedback: Peer state matters, but it does not replace the AND evaluation.

choices.text: The route map with the lower sequence number overrides the other map.
choices.feedback: Sequence order is internal to a route map; it does not turn multiple condition maps into precedence rules.

questions.stem: An IPv6 advertise-map references an IPv4 condition map, and cross-family-conditional-adv is disabled. How is that IPv4 condition treated?

choices.text: It is evaluated against the global routing table.
choices.feedback: The feature does not fall back to the general routing table for cross-family matching.

choices.text: It is evaluated against the IPv4 RIB automatically.
choices.feedback: Automatic cross-family lookup is disabled by default.

choices.text: It is ignored only when the IPv6 peer is down.
choices.feedback: The mismatch is an address-family/RIB issue, not a peer-state exception.

choices.text: It is absent from the IPv6 RIB and therefore fails an exist condition.
choices.feedback: Without cross-family evaluation, the IPv4 route is not found in the IPv6 RIB.

questions.stem: Which object determines the route eligible for export, rather than the condition that gates the export?

choices.text: The condition route map.
choices.feedback: It describes the route predicate used to decide whether advertisement is allowed.

choices.text: The advertise route map.
choices.feedback: It defines what is eligible to be advertised after the condition gate passes.

choices.text: The neighbor route reflector client flag.
choices.feedback: That changes BGP reflection behavior, not the conditional export payload.

choices.text: The local preference attribute.
choices.feedback: Local preference influences path selection inside an AS, not the conditional advertise-map definition.

questions.stem: An administrator clicks Activate on FCT_IPsec_Recommended and enters the client pool and PSK. What object should be assigned to managed devices afterward?

choices.text: The factory seed, because activation only changes its parameters.
choices.feedback: Activation creates a new editable template rather than mutating the factory seed.

choices.text: The generated editable template created by activation.
choices.feedback: The generated instance carries the site values and is the object assigned for deployment.

choices.text: The IPsec phase-2 selector directly from the ADOM database.
choices.feedback: The template is the provisioning object; device configuration is produced at install time.

choices.text: The FortiClient EMS endpoint group.
choices.feedback: EMS endpoint groups do not replace FortiManager IPsec provisioning templates.

questions.stem: A remote-access FortiClient VPN is being provisioned. Which recommended template matches that role?

choices.text: HUB_IPSec_Recommended.
choices.feedback: That template is for the hub role in a site-to-site overlay design.

choices.text: Branch_IPSec_Recommended.
choices.feedback: That template is intended for a branch role, not the FortiClient remote-access client template.

choices.text: FortiGate-HA-Recommended.
choices.feedback: HA templates do not define the FortiClient dial-up VPN workflow.

choices.text: FCT_IPsec_Recommended.
choices.feedback: This is the recommended template intended for FortiClient VPN tunnels.

questions.stem: An IPsec template-generated interface is referenced by another object, but the device is no longer assigned to the template. Install preview fails. What is the safest first correction?

choices.text: Restore the device/template assignment or remove stale references after checking consumers.
choices.feedback: The generated interface and its consumers must remain consistent with the template assignment scope.

choices.text: Delete the VDOM and recreate the VPN interface.
choices.feedback: That is destructive and does not address the missing template ownership.

choices.text: Change the IKE proposal until preview succeeds.
choices.feedback: IKE proposals are unrelated to a FortiManager object-reference/install-preview failure.

choices.text: Disable the FortiGate management tunnel.
choices.feedback: Management reachability does not resolve the missing template-generated interface reference.

questions.stem: The install preview contains the intended VPN objects and the install task succeeds, but the remote client cannot establish IKE. What does the successful install prove?

choices.text: The remote client has accepted the phase-1 proposal.
choices.feedback: Installation proves configuration delivery, not remote peer acceptance.

choices.text: The VPN is fully operational end to end.
choices.feedback: IKE negotiation and data-plane reachability still require independent verification.

choices.text: FortiManager delivered the intended configuration to the target.
choices.feedback: The preview and install task establish delivery, not tunnel establishment.

choices.text: The client address pool is reachable through every firewall policy.
choices.feedback: Reachability and policy are not proved by configuration installation.

questions.stem: Which HA mode is supported for a FortiAnalyzer Fabric Supervisor pair in 8.0.0?

choices.text: Active-passive only.
choices.feedback: The supervisor feature explicitly excludes active-active operation.

choices.text: Active-active with split member ownership.
choices.feedback: The documented supervisor design uses one active control owner.

choices.text: Active-active with shared Fabric Settings.
choices.feedback: Configuration synchronization does not imply concurrent member control.

choices.text: Standalone with manual member failover.
choices.feedback: The new feature is an HA pair, not a manual-only recovery procedure.

questions.stem: Before failover, the secondary shows the Fabric topology but no direct member connections. What is the best interpretation?

choices.text: Member authorization failed on the secondary.
choices.feedback: The standby is not expected to establish member connections before promotion.

choices.text: The topology database is corrupt.
choices.feedback: A synchronized topology can be present even while member sessions are owned by the primary.

choices.text: This is the documented standby behavior.
choices.feedback: The secondary receives Fabric Settings but waits until promotion to connect to members.

choices.text: The cluster is running active-active unexpectedly.
choices.feedback: Active-active is not supported for supervisor HA.

questions.stem: Which field most directly shows whether the Fabric supervisor configuration has synchronized to the secondary?

choices.text: Member authorization state.
choices.feedback: Authorization is a member-management action, not the supervisor synchronization indicator.

choices.text: Supervisor Data Sync.
choices.feedback: This supervisor-specific column reports synchronization state.

choices.text: Report Worker queue depth.
choices.feedback: That measures report processing, not Fabric supervisor replication.

choices.text: FortiView session count.
choices.feedback: A view count does not prove supervisor configuration synchronization.

questions.stem: After the secondary is promoted, what should happen to Fabric member connections?

choices.text: Members remain pinned to the former primary until manual reauthorization.
choices.feedback: The documented failover behavior is automatic member reconnection to the new primary.

choices.text: Members form independent active-active sessions to both nodes.
choices.feedback: Supervisor HA is active-passive and has one active member-control owner.

choices.text: Only log forwarding resumes; Fabric Settings must be rebuilt.
choices.feedback: The Fabric Settings are synchronized and member reconnection is automatic.

choices.text: Members automatically reconnect to the new primary and data sync follows.
choices.feedback: That is the documented supervisor failover sequence.

questions.stem: A newly attached 802.3at endpoint is denied power on a nearly full switch. Which reservation should be considered first?

choices.text: The 36 W dynamic guard band for AT mode.
choices.feedback: FortiSwitch reserves the maximum expected power for the device type before enabling the port.

choices.text: The endpoint's measured idle draw only.
choices.feedback: Admission uses the documented guard band, not just momentary idle consumption.

choices.text: The LLDP neighbor's VLAN assignment.
choices.feedback: VLAN selection does not determine the PoE budget reservation.

choices.text: The port's spanning-tree forwarding delay.
choices.feedback: STP state does not explain PoE power admission.

questions.stem: The switch must preserve power to existing endpoints and deny new ones when the budget is exhausted. Which allocation behavior matches that intent?

choices.text: Priority allocation with lower-numbered ports disabled first.
choices.feedback: Priority mode sheds higher-numbered ports first when more power is needed.

choices.text: First-come, first-served allocation.
choices.feedback: FCFS preserves connected devices and denies new devices when budget is insufficient.

choices.text: FCFS with a critical-priority override on all ports.
choices.feedback: FCFS does not use the same priority ordering as priority allocation.

choices.text: Dynamic guard band disabled globally.
choices.feedback: Removing the reservation is not the documented FCFS behavior and risks overcommit.

questions.stem: The global switch policy is FCFS, but one physical port is configured for priority allocation. Which setting wins for that port?

choices.text: The global policy always wins.
choices.feedback: The guide states the physical-port setting takes precedence.

choices.text: The newest LLDP advertisement wins.
choices.feedback: LLDP does not choose the PoE allocation policy.

choices.text: The physical-port setting takes precedence.
choices.feedback: Per-port configuration overrides the global allocation setting.

choices.text: The endpoint's negotiated power class wins.
choices.feedback: Power class affects reservation, not policy precedence.

questions.stem: Which output is most useful to determine whether a specific port is delivering power and what class was detected?

choices.text: get switch poe inline only.
choices.feedback: That is a switch-level capacity view, not the per-port status evidence.

choices.text: diagnose switch lldp neighbors port12.
choices.feedback: LLDP neighbor data does not prove the PSE is delivering power.

choices.text: get system performance status.
choices.feedback: System performance does not show the port's PoE electrical state.

choices.text: diagnose switch poe status port12.
choices.feedback: The per-port output reports power state, PD type, class, voltage, current, and priority.

questions.stem: An AP has a configured Static LoWi position and a working GNSS receiver. Which source is used?

choices.text: GNSS because it is more accurate than manual coordinates.
choices.feedback: The documented precedence places user input ahead of GNSS.

choices.text: Static LoWi because user input has highest priority.
choices.feedback: Manual coordinates override GNSS and calculated LoWi.

choices.text: Calculated LoWi because it always overrides other sources.
choices.feedback: Calculated LoWi is the fallback after static and GNSS.

choices.text: The nearest responder's coordinates only.
choices.feedback: A responder provides a reference point, not the initiator's final location.

questions.stem: What is the documented minimum AP topology for a complete LoWi calculation?

choices.text: One initiator and two responders.
choices.feedback: Two ranges are insufficient for the documented 3D trilateration design.

choices.text: Three initiators and one responder.
choices.feedback: The design requires one initiator and multiple known-position responders.

choices.text: One initiator and four known-position responders.
choices.feedback: Four responders plus one initiator provide the documented five-AP minimum.

choices.text: Two initiators and two GPS-only APs.
choices.feedback: The calculation needs four responders and one initiator.

questions.stem: Where should 802.11mc RTT measurement be enabled for the documented LoWi configuration?

choices.text: On the 5-GHz radio of the relevant WTP profiles.
choices.feedback: Fortinet restricts the 802.11mc measurement configuration to 5 GHz for accuracy and reliability.

choices.text: On every 2.4-GHz radio only.
choices.feedback: The documented configuration does not use 2.4 GHz for RTT measurement.

choices.text: On the 6-GHz radio only.
choices.feedback: The 8.0 guide specifies 5 GHz for 802.11mc measurement.

choices.text: On the Ethernet uplink interface.
choices.feedback: 802.11mc is a wireless RTT capability, not an Ethernet setting.

questions.stem: A FortiGate diagnostic shows lowi-pos-type: gps. What does this prove?

choices.text: The AP has completed 802.11mc trilateration.
choices.feedback: The source field identifies GNSS, not calculated LoWi.

choices.text: Four responder APs are operational and accurate.
choices.feedback: GPS source selection does not prove the responder topology.

choices.text: The AP is using manually entered coordinates.
choices.feedback: Static position is a separate source value and does not prove that 802.11mc ranging completed.

choices.text: The active coordinates came from the AP's GNSS source.
choices.feedback: The field identifies the source; it does not validate LoWi ranging.

questions.stem: FortiNAC can query LDAP users, but Winbind domain join fails against FreeIPA. What is the correct interpretation?

choices.text: The LDAP server password is necessarily incorrect.
choices.feedback: LDAP queries can succeed while an AD-specific domain join fails.

choices.text: FreeIPA must be configured with a different NetBIOS short name.
choices.feedback: The documented Join Domain operation performs a Samba AD join, which FreeIPA does not accept.

choices.text: Winbind Join Domain is an Active Directory join, not a generic LDAP/Kerberos bind.
choices.feedback: Keep directory synchronization and AD domain membership as separate integration paths.

choices.text: FortiNAC must be changed to local-only authentication.
choices.feedback: LDAP-based user/group functions can remain available without Winbind AD join.

questions.stem: Why would an administrator upload a Kerberos keytab for Local Winbind configuration?

choices.text: To perform the AD join without retaining the administrator password in the workflow.
choices.feedback: The keytab supplies principal key material for the domain-join operation.

choices.text: To replace the LDAP directory with local user accounts.
choices.feedback: A keytab does not replace directory synchronization.

choices.text: To encrypt all RADIUS Access-Requests between switches and FortiNAC.
choices.feedback: That is not the documented purpose of the Winbind keytab.

choices.text: To synchronize FortiNAC appliance clocks with domain controllers.
choices.feedback: Time synchronization is a separate prerequisite, not the keytab function.

questions.stem: Which field should contain CORP in a domain named corp.example.com?

choices.text: Kerberos realm name.
choices.feedback: The Kerberos realm is the DNS-style domain name.

choices.text: Domain NetBIOS name.
choices.feedback: The NetBIOS domain is the short name; the realm is corp.example.com.

choices.text: Domain controller hostname.
choices.feedback: That field expects a controller host name or supported selector.

choices.text: Local appliance FQDN.
choices.feedback: The local appliance name is not the domain's short NetBIOS identifier.

questions.stem: A successful LDAP search is observed after a Winbind change. What has not yet been proved?

choices.text: That the LDAP directory is reachable.
choices.feedback: The search is direct evidence of directory reachability.

choices.text: That user attributes can be read.
choices.feedback: The search confirms the queried attributes were returned.

choices.text: That the selected LDAP server accepted the query.
choices.feedback: The successful search proves that request completed.

choices.text: That the appliance is joined to AD and Kerberos authentication works.
choices.feedback: LDAP reachability is separate from Winbind domain trust and ticket validation.

questions.stem: An isolated endpoint queries an FQDN that is not in Allowed Domains. What DNS answer should it normally receive?

choices.text: The production resolver's answer from an iterative lookup.
choices.feedback: Unlisted names follow the isolation/captive path rather than production forwarding.

choices.text: NXDOMAIN from the authoritative DNS server.
choices.feedback: The documented behavior returns the isolation-interface address for unlisted domains.

choices.text: The FortiNAC isolation-interface address.
choices.feedback: FortiNAC returns its service-interface address unless the domain is allowed.

choices.text: The default gateway address for the isolation VLAN.
choices.feedback: The gateway is not the DNS proxy's redirect address.

questions.stem: An organization adds microsoft.com to Allowed Domains. Which scope does that entry provide?

choices.text: The parent domain and its subdomains.
choices.feedback: The guide states that adding a large parent domain includes subdomains.

choices.text: Only the exact microsoft.com hostname.
choices.feedback: A parent entry is broader than a single exact host.

choices.text: Every domain hosted by Microsoft's authoritative DNS servers.
choices.feedback: DNS delegation does not make unrelated zones part of the allowlist.

choices.text: Only the first-level subdomain under microsoft.com.
choices.feedback: The documented parent-domain entry includes all subdomains.

questions.stem: After a DNS query resolves to a production IP, the isolated endpoint still cannot connect. What should be checked next?

choices.text: Add more DNS wildcards until the connection succeeds.
choices.feedback: The allowlist has already produced a production answer; wildcards are unsupported.

choices.text: Isolation VLAN routing and firewall policy to the destination.
choices.feedback: FortiNAC is not a router; DNS forwarding does not create network reachability.

choices.text: Change the DNS response to the FortiNAC interface.
choices.feedback: That would return the endpoint to the captive path.

choices.text: Disable DHCP on the isolation network.
choices.feedback: The correct DNS answer does not implicate DHCP by itself.

questions.stem: Which Allowed Domains entry is explicitly unsafe because it can break FortiNAC agent connectivity?

choices.text: A required antivirus update domain.
choices.feedback: A vendor update domain is a legitimate allowlist target when an isolated host needs that service.

choices.text: A production DNS server IP address.
choices.feedback: The server address belongs in the DNS-forwarder field, not the domain list.

choices.text: A parent vendor domain used for software updates.
choices.feedback: That may be intentionally allowed for isolated hosts.

choices.text: The parent domain of the FortiNAC appliance's own FQDN.
choices.feedback: Fortinet warns this can create asymmetric routing and prevent agent TCP sessions.

questions.stem: A TACACS+ authorization rule was changed, but a logged-in operator still has the old command rights. What is the documented default explanation?

choices.text: The device caches the user's privilege level forever.
choices.feedback: The documented cache is a FortiAuthenticator authorization session with a finite lifetime.

choices.text: The authorization session can remain valid for 28,800 seconds.
choices.feedback: Rule changes do not apply to the existing session until it expires.

choices.text: The authentication password was not rotated.
choices.feedback: Password rotation does not force authorization-session re-evaluation.

choices.text: The TACACS+ client IP must be re-added to the policy.
choices.feedback: Client matching is a separate stage from post-auth authorization-session caching.

questions.stem: A shell command is permitted, but a dangerous argument should be blocked. Where should the restriction be defined?

choices.text: In the TACACS+ client object.
choices.feedback: The client object identifies the device, not command arguments.

choices.text: In the global RADIUS attribute list.
choices.feedback: RADIUS attributes do not define TACACS+ shell-command argument policy.

choices.text: In the shell-command object included by the authorization rule.
choices.feedback: The shell-command object defines command and allowed/denied argument sets.

choices.text: In the FortiGate local-in policy.
choices.feedback: Local-in policy controls traffic to the firewall, not TACACS+ command authorization.

questions.stem: A non-shell service returns a mandatory attribute the network device cannot understand. What is the expected result?

choices.text: Authorization can fail because mandatory AVPs must be understood and honored.
choices.feedback: A mandatory attribute is not optional metadata; the receiver must act on it.

choices.text: The device silently ignores the attribute and grants access.
choices.feedback: That behavior is documented for optional, not mandatory, attributes.

choices.text: FortiAuthenticator converts the attribute to a shell command.
choices.feedback: Non-shell service AVPs are not transformed into command rules.

choices.text: The TACACS+ authentication phase restarts with PAP.
choices.feedback: The failure occurs in authorization response handling, not authentication method negotiation.

questions.stem: Which rule scope is supported for TACACS+ authorization rules?

choices.text: Only the TACACS+ client IP address.
choices.feedback: Client matching and user authorization are distinct objects.

choices.text: Only an individual local administrator account.
choices.feedback: Rules can also be assigned within user groups.

choices.text: Only the global default rule.
choices.feedback: The guide supports per-user and user-group assignment.

choices.text: A user group or an individual user account.
choices.feedback: Both scopes are documented for authorization rules.

questions.stem: A target API returns a CSRF cookie during login. What must the next password-change request do?

choices.text: Ignore the cookie because the session is already authenticated.
choices.feedback: Authentication does not remove the target's CSRF requirement.

choices.text: Store the cookie only in the report log.
choices.feedback: Logging the token does not replay it in the change request.

choices.text: Extract the token into $CSRFTOKEN and send it where the API expects it.
choices.feedback: The changer can extract the CSRF token and reuse it in the subsequent request.

choices.text: Convert the cookie value into a URL path.
choices.feedback: The token must be placed in the API's expected header or body field.

questions.stem: Which step type evaluates a prior HTTP response and can extract cookies or tokens?

choices.text: Execute.
choices.feedback: Execute is the request-sending step; response matching and token extraction belong in Expect.

choices.text: Expect.
choices.feedback: Expect validates response status/body and can extract cookies or tokens.

choices.text: Verifier only.
choices.feedback: The verifier proves the final credential; it is not the response-matching step.

choices.text: Jump.
choices.feedback: Jump controls sequence branching rather than response evaluation itself.

questions.stem: The API returns HTTP 200 with a nested JSON object containing an application error. What is the correct next action?

choices.text: Mark the password change successful because the HTTP code is 200.
choices.feedback: Transport success does not prove application-level password change success.

choices.text: Retry the same request repeatedly without inspecting the body.
choices.feedback: Repeated requests can lock the account and hide the actual error.

choices.text: Disable the verifier so the changer can complete.
choices.feedback: The verifier is the independent safety check for the new credential.

choices.text: Parse the correct nested JSON path and require the target's success condition.
choices.feedback: The Web-API changer supports multi-layer JSON parsing; use the actual response structure.

questions.stem: What is the strongest proof that a password rotation succeeded?

choices.text: A verifier authenticates to the target using the new credential.
choices.feedback: The verifier proves the new secret works, beyond an HTTP success response.

choices.text: The password-change POST returned any 2xx status.
choices.feedback: A 2xx response can still contain an application error or pending job.

choices.text: The CSRF token was extracted successfully.
choices.feedback: Token extraction proves session setup, not credential change.

choices.text: The changer advanced to its final sequence step.
choices.feedback: Sequence completion is not a substitute for target-side credential verification.

questions.stem: A report has a template assigned directly to it and another template assigned to its folder. Which template is used?

choices.text: The report-specific template.
choices.feedback: Report-level assignment has the highest precedence.

choices.text: The folder template because it contains more reports.
choices.feedback: Folder scope is used only when the report has no specific template.

choices.text: The root system template because it is always authoritative.
choices.feedback: Root is the final fallback when report and folder templates are absent.

choices.text: The most recently modified template regardless of scope.
choices.feedback: Template resolution is based on scope precedence, not modification time.

questions.stem: A pre-7.0 upgrade stalls on first login with a report-template migration message. Custom folder templates are present. What should be inspected first?

choices.text: The ClickHouse event integrity configuration.
choices.feedback: That is unrelated to report-template migration.

choices.text: The report query's time range.
choices.feedback: The migration issue concerns unsupported template scope, not query results.

choices.text: Custom Report Design Templates assigned to report folders.
choices.feedback: Folder-level custom templates are not supported in 7.0.0 migration and can block conversion.

choices.text: The Collector event parsing rules.
choices.feedback: Parsing rules do not govern PDF template conversion.

questions.stem: During migration, how are four or more charts from one report laid out in the new Visual Report Designer format?

choices.text: Four charts in one row with separate legends.
choices.feedback: The migration normalizes charts into two-per-row layout.

choices.text: Two charts per row with a common legend at the end.
choices.feedback: That is the documented conversion for four or more charts.

choices.text: One chart per page with a repeated cover.
choices.feedback: That is not the documented multi-chart conversion.

choices.text: All charts are removed and replaced with a table.
choices.feedback: The migration preserves chart content with a normalized layout.

questions.stem: In a Service Provider deployment, where can report templates be defined?

choices.text: At each customer folder independently.
choices.feedback: The documented SP scope restricts template definition to Super/Global.

choices.text: Only at the report level for every tenant.
choices.feedback: Report-level assignment is not the only allowed scope in ordinary deployments.

choices.text: At each Worker node separately.
choices.feedback: Workers do not own tenant report-template scope.

choices.text: At Super/Global level, applying across customers.
choices.feedback: The guide specifies Super/Global-only template definition for Service Provider deployments.

questions.stem: A local DNS domain entry is set to Allow. What happens next in the documented pipeline?

choices.text: FortiGuard category rating always overrides it.
choices.feedback: Local Allow is terminal and bypasses category evaluation.

choices.text: The request is redirected to the block portal.
choices.feedback: Block is the local action that redirects the DNS response to the block portal.

choices.text: The request bypasses FortiGuard category evaluation.
choices.feedback: Local Allow is terminal; Monitor, by contrast, continues to category rating.

choices.text: DNS translation is automatically disabled for the entire profile.
choices.feedback: Allow precedence does not disable the separate translation feature.

questions.stem: A domain is locally allowed, but resolution fails because its authoritative name servers belong to a blocked category. Why?

choices.text: The authoritative nameserver hostnames generate separate DNS queries that are rated independently.
choices.feedback: Allowing the requested domain does not automatically allow the NS hostnames it depends on.

choices.text: The DNS Filter ignores all local entries when a CNAME exists.
choices.feedback: The failure can occur on the independent nameserver lookup, not because local rules are ignored.

choices.text: The FortiSASE resolver requires a static route for every NS record.
choices.feedback: DNS category evaluation is separate from routing.

choices.text: The client has to use TCP port 853 for all DNS requests.
choices.feedback: The scenario is about independent DNS names and category filtering, not a universal DoT requirement.

questions.stem: A DNS translation entry maps the original resolved IP to an internal address. What does this not create?

choices.text: A DNS response containing the translated address.
choices.feedback: That is the purpose of the translation entry.

choices.text: A route or firewall permission to the translated server.
choices.feedback: Address substitution does not create network reachability or security policy.

choices.text: A change to the authoritative DNS zone.
choices.feedback: Translation occurs in the DNS Filter response path, not in the authoritative zone.

choices.text: A new FortiGuard category.
choices.feedback: Translation is an address rewrite, not a category assignment.

questions.stem: What is the consequence of enabling the DNS Filter rating-error fail-open option?

choices.text: DNS requests are always blocked when FortiGuard is unreachable.
choices.feedback: Fail-closed would deny requests when rating fails; fail-open deliberately permits them.

choices.text: Only local domain entries continue to resolve.
choices.feedback: The option permits DNS requests when FortiGuard rating fails.

choices.text: The resolver switches automatically to proxy mode.
choices.feedback: Proxy mode is outside the supported DNS Filter path, not an alternate DNS failover behavior.

choices.text: DNS requests are allowed during FortiGuard rating failure and a log is recorded.
choices.feedback: Fail-open is an availability choice that permits DNS when rating services fail.

questions.stem: What is the default value of the SD-WAN service hold-down timer?

choices.text: 15 seconds.
choices.feedback: Fifteen seconds is an example value, not the default.

choices.text: 30 seconds.
choices.feedback: The default is zero seconds, so no extra delay applies until an administrator configures one.

choices.text: 0 seconds.
choices.feedback: Without an explicit value, there is no additional recovery hold-down.

choices.text: 120 seconds.
choices.feedback: The timer range is much broader and defaults to zero.

questions.stem: A shortcut tunnel recovers and appears alive, but the service keeps it at low priority for 15 seconds. What is happening?

choices.text: The recovered member is in its configured hold-down interval.
choices.feedback: The feature delays normal priority restoration after recovery.

choices.text: The tunnel has failed phase-2 negotiation.
choices.feedback: An alive member with a running hold timer is not evidence of phase-2 failure.

choices.text: The SLA probe has been disabled permanently.
choices.feedback: The hold-down timer is a temporary priority state, not a permanent probe setting.

choices.text: The route has been withdrawn from BGP.
choices.feedback: The diagnostic evidence is service-member priority, not necessarily BGP withdrawal.

questions.stem: An operator expects hold-down to delay failback in an SLA-mode service. What should be verified first?

choices.text: The tunnel's phase-1 lifetime.
choices.feedback: IKE lifetime does not establish service-strategy timer applicability.

choices.text: The actual SD-WAN service mode and release-specific applicability.
choices.feedback: Community guidance notes the timer is not applicable for SLA mode; inspect the strategy before tuning.

choices.text: The branch DHCP lease time.
choices.feedback: DHCP lease behavior is unrelated to service hold-down.

choices.text: The FortiAnalyzer supervisor role.
choices.feedback: Supervisor HA does not determine SD-WAN service strategy behavior.

questions.stem: Which output best proves the hold-down timer is running for a service?

choices.text: get router info bgp summary.
choices.feedback: BGP summary does not show the SD-WAN member hold timer.

choices.text: diagnose vpn ike gateway list.
choices.feedback: IKE state does not show service-member priority timing.

choices.text: diagnose sys sdwan health-check.
choices.feedback: Health-check output measures probe state, not the service hold-down fields.

choices.text: diagnose sys sdwan service4 showing Hold down time, Hold start, and now.
choices.feedback: The service diagnostic exposes the timer and selected-member state.

questions.stem: An isolated FortiNAC-F host cannot reach its identity provider. Its DNS query for the IdP FQDN returns the FortiNAC port2 address. Which action best preserves the intended isolation design?

choices.text: Disable all DNS filtering and route the host directly to production.
choices.feedback: That removes the isolation control rather than correcting the specific DNS dependency.

choices.text: Add the required IdP FQDN and CNAME targets to Allowed Domains and verify production DNS.
choices.feedback: The allowlist causes FortiNAC to forward the name while the host remains in isolation.

choices.text: Change the endpoint's default gateway to the FortiNAC service interface.
choices.feedback: FortiNAC supplies the isolation DNS response but does not route the endpoint's subsequent traffic.

choices.text: Add the IdP to the FortiNAC host registration group only.
choices.feedback: Registration state does not change the DNS proxy allowlist.

questions.stem: A FortiAnalyzer standby shows the replicated Fabric topology, while FortiSIEM PDF exports use the wrong layout. Which pair of checks addresses the actual independent control planes?

choices.text: Check FortiAnalyzer member connections on standby and change the SIEM query time range.
choices.feedback: Standby member connections are not expected before promotion, and query time range does not set PDF template precedence.

choices.text: Enable active-active supervisor mode and edit the FortiSIEM collector parser.
choices.feedback: Active-active supervisor mode is unsupported; collector parsing does not fix PDF layout.

choices.text: Verify Supervisor Data Sync and inspect report/folder/root template precedence.
choices.feedback: One check validates supervisor replication; the other resolves the PDF template selection.

choices.text: Rebuild the FortiAnalyzer Fabric and recreate all SIEM report bundles.
choices.feedback: Both actions are destructive and skip the documented diagnostic evidence.
